insider_note: This integral is the area of a quarter circle of radius a, which is why the answer πa²/4 has such a familiar geometric shape.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Apply the standard formula
steps.margin_note: First mark. ∫√(a²−x²)dx = (x/2)√(a²−x²) + (a²/2)Sin⁻¹(x/a) + c — a standard formula to know.
steps.memory_tip: The formula always pairs an algebraic term with a Sin⁻¹ term — never just one or the other.
steps.why: √(a²−x²) has a standard antiderivative built from two pieces — an algebraic term and an inverse-sine term — that is worth memorising rather than deriving by a trigonometric substitution each time.
common_mistakes: Misremembering the formula and dropping the (a²/2)Sin⁻¹(x/a) term.
Writing Sin⁻¹(x/a) as Sin⁻¹(a/x) by mistake.

steps.label: Apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Sin⁻¹(1) = π/2 — memorise this standard value.
steps.memory_tip: At x=a the square root itself becomes 0, so only the inverse-sine half of the formula contributes.

lines.text: Check: y = √(a² − x²) from 0 to a is a

steps.why: At the upper limit x=a, √(a²−x²) becomes 0 so only the Sin⁻¹ term survives, giving (a²/2)Sin⁻¹(1)=(a²/2)(π/2); the lower limit x=0 contributes nothing since both terms vanish.
common_mistakes: Using Sin⁻¹(1) = π instead of the correct π/2.
Forgetting that the algebraic term (x/2)√(a²−x²) vanishes at x=a because √(a²−a²)=0.
